prompt: Write a function `two_sum(nums, target)` that returns the indices [i, j] (i < j) of the two numbers in `nums` that add up to `target`. Assume exactly one solution exists. Then explain the time and space complexity of your approach.

rubric.description: States O(n) time with a hash map (or justifies the complexity of the chosen approach)
rubric.hint: Can you avoid checking every pair? What lookup structure is O(1)?
rubric.follow_up: Your solution's complexity wasn't fully explained. What are the time and space complexity, and how would a hash map change them?

rubric.description: Considers duplicates / negative numbers / same element not used twice
rubric.hint: What happens if the same value appears twice?
rubric.follow_up: How does your solution handle duplicate values such as nums=[3,3], target=6?

hints: Store each number's index as you iterate.
For each x, check whether target - x was already seen.

prompt: Write `is_valid(s)` that returns True if the string of brackets `()[]{}` is balanced and correctly nested, otherwise False. Explain your approach and its complexity.

rubric.description: Uses a stack and explains why
rubric.hint: Which data structure gives you the most recently opened bracket?
rubric.follow_up: Why is a stack the right data structure here?

rubric.description: States O(n) time and O(n) space
rubric.hint: How many times is each character processed?
rubric.follow_up: What is the worst-case space usage and when does it happen?

hints: Push opening brackets; on a closing bracket, check the top of the stack.

prompt: Write `merge(intervals)` that merges all overlapping intervals (lists of [start, end]) and returns the merged list sorted by start. Explain the complexity.

rubric.description: Sorts by start then merges in one pass
rubric.hint: What if the intervals were sorted by start time?
rubric.follow_up: Why does sorting first make a single pass sufficient?

rubric.description: States O(n log n) due to sorting
rubric.hint: What dominates: the sort or the merge pass?
rubric.follow_up: What is the overall time complexity and which step dominates it?

hints: Sort intervals by start.
Compare each interval with the last merged interval.

prompt: Write `top_k_frequent(nums, k)` returning the k most frequent elements (any order). Discuss at least two approaches and their complexity.

rubric.description: Discusses counting plus heap or bucket sort
rubric.hint: Count first, then think about how to pick the k largest counts.
rubric.follow_up: How would a heap of size k or bucket sort improve on fully sorting the counts?

rubric.description: Correct complexity for the chosen approach
rubric.hint: What does each approach cost in time?
rubric.follow_up: What is the time complexity of the heap-based approach?

hints: collections.Counter gives you frequencies.
heapq.nlargest(k, ...) keeps only k items.

prompt: Write `search(nums, target)` that returns the index of `target` in the sorted list `nums`, or -1 if absent, in O(log n) time. Explain how you avoid off-by-one errors.

rubric.hint: Define what the range [lo, hi] means at every iteration.
rubric.follow_up: What invariant does your loop maintain, and when does it terminate?

rubric.hint: How much of the search space is removed each step?
rubric.follow_up: Why is the complexity logarithmic?

hints: Use lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1 and loop while lo <= hi.

prompt: How would you implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put? Describe the data structures and what happens on a get, a put, and an eviction.

rubric.description: Hash map plus doubly linked list (or OrderedDict)
rubric.hint: You need O(1) lookup and O(1) reordering. Which two structures give you each?
rubric.follow_up: Why does the list need to be doubly linked?

rubric.description: Explains move-to-front on access and eviction of the tail
rubric.hint: What happens to an entry's position when it is read?
rubric.follow_up: Walk through exactly what happens when the cache is full and a new key is inserted.

rubric.hint: Which operations would be O(n) with a plain list?
rubric.follow_up: Which part of your design guarantees O(1) for eviction?

hints: Map keys to list nodes.
Keep most recently used at the head.

prompt: Given an unweighted graph, how do you find the shortest path between two nodes? How does your answer change if edges have non-negative weights?

rubric.description: BFS for unweighted graphs with a queue and visited set
rubric.hint: Which traversal explores nodes in order of distance?
rubric.follow_up: Why does BFS guarantee the shortest path in an unweighted graph but DFS does not?

rubric.description: Dijkstra with a priority queue for weighted graphs
rubric.hint: What algorithm handles non-negative weights?
rubric.follow_up: What is Dijkstra's time complexity with a binary heap?

rubric.hint: Each vertex and edge is processed how many times?
rubric.follow_up: What is the complexity of BFS in terms of vertices and edges?

hints: Think about exploring the graph level by level.

prompt: What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in CPython, and how does it affect choosing between threads, processes and asyncio?

rubric.description: One thread executes Python bytecode at a time
rubric.hint: What does the lock protect?
rubric.follow_up: What exactly does the GIL prevent two threads from doing at the same time?

rubric.description: Threads help I/O-bound work, processes for CPU-bound
rubric.hint: Does the GIL get released while waiting on I/O?
rubric.follow_up: For a CPU-heavy image-processing job, would you use threads or processes, and why?

rubric.description: asyncio as cooperative concurrency on one thread
rubric.hint: How does asyncio achieve concurrency without threads?
rubric.follow_up: When would asyncio be a better choice than threads?

hints: Separate CPU-bound and I/O-bound workloads.

prompt: Explain the difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression. When would you prefer a generator?

rubric.description: Generators are lazy and produce values on demand
rubric.hint: When is each value computed?
rubric.follow_up: What happens if you iterate over the same generator twice?

rubric.description: Memory efficiency for large or infinite sequences
rubric.hint: What happens with a billion items?
rubric.follow_up: Give an example where a list would run out of memory but a generator would not.

rubric.description: Lists support indexing / reuse; generators are single-pass
rubric.hint: What can a list do that a generator cannot?
rubric.follow_up: What operations do you lose with a generator?

hints: Think about when values are computed and stored.

prompt: What is wrong with `def add_item(item, items=[]): items.append(item); return items`? How do you fix it?

rubric.description: Default evaluated once at definition time and shared
rubric.hint: When is the default value created?
rubric.follow_up: When exactly is the default list created, and why does that matter?

rubric.description: Use None as default and create a new list inside
rubric.hint: What sentinel can you use instead?
rubric.follow_up: Show the corrected function signature and first line.

rubric.hint: Would the same problem occur with a tuple default?
rubric.follow_up: Why is a tuple default safe?

hints: Call the function twice without the second argument and compare.

prompt: What is a decorator in Python? Describe how you would write one that measures how long a function takes, and what `functools.wraps` is for.

rubric.description: A callable that takes a function and returns a wrapped function
rubric.hint: What does @decorator desugar to?
rubric.follow_up: What does `@timer` above `def f()` translate to?

rubric.hint: How does the wrapper accept arbitrary arguments?
rubric.follow_up: How does your wrapper pass through arguments and the return value?

rubric.hint: What happens to f.__name__ after decorating?
rubric.follow_up: What breaks if you omit functools.wraps?

hints: Decorators are functions returning functions.

prompt: A client may retry a POST /payments request after a timeout. How do you make this endpoint safe against duplicate charges?

rubric.hint: How can the server recognize a retry of the same request?
rubric.follow_up: Where would you store idempotency keys and for how long?

rubric.description: Persist key with result and return stored response on retry
rubric.hint: What should the second request return?
rubric.follow_up: What do you return if the first request is still in progress when the retry arrives?

rubric.description: Unique constraint / lock to handle concurrent retries
rubric.hint: What if two retries arrive at the same time?
rubric.follow_up: How do you prevent a race between two identical concurrent requests?

hints: GET and PUT are idempotent by definition; POST is not.

prompt: A query `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 AND status = 'open' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` is slow on a table with 50M rows. How would you investigate and fix it?

rubric.description: Uses EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE to inspect the plan
rubric.hint: How do you see what the database is actually doing?
rubric.follow_up: What would you look for in the EXPLAIN ANALYZE output?

rubric.description: Composite index matching filter and sort columns
rubric.hint: Can one index serve both the WHERE and ORDER BY?
rubric.follow_up: In what column order would you create the index, and why?

rubric.description: Index costs: write overhead, partial indexes, selectivity
rubric.hint: What do indexes cost?
rubric.follow_up: When would a partial index on status = 'open' be a better choice?

hints: Start with the query plan.
Think about which columns are filtered and sorted.

prompt: Two requests try to reserve the last seat on a flight at the same time. How do you prevent overbooking at the database level?

rubric.hint: What groups the read and write together?
rubric.follow_up: Is a transaction alone enough at the default isolation level? Why or why not?

rubric.description: Row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), conditional update, or constraint
rubric.hint: How can the second request be forced to wait or fail?
rubric.follow_up: Compare pessimistic locking with an optimistic version-number approach.

rubric.hint: What anomaly occurs at READ COMMITTED?
rubric.follow_up: What would SERIALIZABLE isolation do here?

hints: The danger is the gap between reading the count and writing the reservation.

prompt: Compare session-cookie authentication with JWT bearer tokens for a web app. What are the security trade-offs, and how do you revoke access?

rubric.description: Server-side session state vs self-contained signed token
rubric.hint: Where is the state kept in each model?
rubric.follow_up: What exactly does the server verify on each request with a JWT?

rubric.hint: Where would you store the token in the browser?
rubric.follow_up: Why is storing a JWT in localStorage risky?

rubric.description: Short expiry, refresh tokens, denylist or token versioning
rubric.hint: A JWT is valid until it expires. How do you cut that short?
rubric.follow_up: How would you log a user out of every device immediately?

hints: Consider where state lives and how each is attacked.

prompt: What is the N+1 query problem with ORMs, how do you detect it, and how do you fix it?

rubric.description: One query for the list plus one per item
rubric.hint: Count the queries when rendering 100 orders with their customers.
rubric.follow_up: How many queries run when listing 100 posts with their authors lazily loaded?

rubric.hint: How can related rows be loaded together?
rubric.follow_up: When would you choose a separate IN query over a JOIN?

rubric.description: Query logging, APM, tests asserting query counts
rubric.hint: How would you notice it in development?
rubric.follow_up: How could a test catch an N+1 regression?

hints: Lazy loading inside a loop is the usual cause.

prompt: How would you implement per-user rate limiting (e.g. 100 requests/minute) for an API running on several servers?

rubric.description: Token bucket / sliding window / fixed window
rubric.hint: Name an algorithm that tracks requests over time.
rubric.follow_up: What is the burst behavior of a fixed window compared to a sliding window?

rubric.description: Shared store (Redis) with atomic increments / expiry
rubric.hint: Where is the counter stored if there are many servers?
rubric.follow_up: How do you keep the counter update atomic?

rubric.hint: What should the client receive when limited?
rubric.follow_up: What headers would you send to help clients back off?

hints: Separate the algorithm from where its state lives.

prompt: You add a Redis cache in front of a product-details endpoint. How do you keep cached data consistent when products are updated?

rubric.hint: Who populates the cache and when does it expire?
rubric.follow_up: Compare cache-aside with write-through for this endpoint.

rubric.hint: What should happen to the cache entry on product update?
rubric.follow_up: Why is deleting the key often safer than updating it?

rubric.description: Stale reads, race conditions, thundering herd
rubric.hint: What can go wrong under concurrent reads and writes?
rubric.follow_up: How would you prevent a cache stampede when a hot key expires?

hints: Think about the read path and the write path separately.

prompt: Design a URL shortener handling 100M new links per month and 10x more redirects. Cover the API, ID generation, storage, and how you scale reads.

rubric.hint: Start with read/write ratio and storage estimates.
rubric.follow_up: Roughly how many redirects per second is that, and how much storage over five years?

rubric.description: Base62 encoding / counter / hash with collision handling
rubric.hint: How do you generate a short unique code?
rubric.follow_up: How do you avoid collisions when generating codes on multiple servers?

rubric.hint: What does the access pattern look like?
rubric.follow_up: Why might a key-value store suit this access pattern?

rubric.hint: Redirects dominate. How do you serve them fast?
rubric.follow_up: Which layer would absorb most redirect traffic and why?

hints: Reads vastly outnumber writes.

prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter service used by many internal APIs. Discuss algorithm choice, data store, latency, and failure modes.

rubric.hint: Which algorithm allows controlled bursts?
rubric.follow_up: Why did you pick that algorithm over the alternatives?

rubric.description: Low-latency shared store with atomic operations
rubric.hint: Where do counters live and how are they updated?
rubric.follow_up: How do you keep latency low when every API call checks the limiter?

rubric.hint: What happens if the store is down?
rubric.follow_up: Should the limiter fail open or closed for a payments API? Why?

rubric.hint: How does it scale to millions of keys?
rubric.follow_up: What accuracy do you give up with local counters synced periodically?

hints: Consider correctness vs latency.

prompt: Design a notification system that sends email, SMS and push notifications to millions of users, with retries and user preferences.

rubric.hint: Should the API send notifications synchronously?
rubric.follow_up: Why decouple the API from delivery with a queue?

rubric.description: Retries with backoff, dead-letter queue, idempotency
rubric.hint: What happens when a provider is down?
rubric.follow_up: How do you avoid sending the same notification twice after a retry?

rubric.description: Preference / opt-out checks and rate limits
rubric.hint: How do you respect what users want?
rubric.follow_up: Where in the pipeline do you check preferences, and why there?

rubric.hint: Each channel has different third-party services.
rubric.follow_up: How would you switch providers if one degrades?

hints: Separate accepting a notification from delivering it.

prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate about a technical decision. What did you do and what was the outcome?

rubric.hint: Set the scene in one or two sentences.
rubric.follow_up: Can you give more context: what project, and what was at stake?

rubric.description: Specific actions you took (I, not we)
rubric.hint: What did you personally do?
rubric.follow_up: What specifically did you do to resolve the disagreement?

rubric.hint: How did it end, and what did you take away?
rubric.follow_up: What was the measurable outcome, and what would you do differently?

rubric.description: Shows respect and openness to other views
rubric.hint: How did you treat the other person's view?
rubric.follow_up: How did you make sure your teammate felt heard?

hints: Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

prompt: Describe a time something you built failed in production or missed a deadline. How did you handle it?

rubric.hint: What was your part in it?
rubric.follow_up: What part of the failure was your responsibility?

rubric.hint: What did you do in the first hours?
rubric.follow_up: How did you communicate the problem to stakeholders?

rubric.hint: How did you stop it from happening again?
rubric.follow_up: What concrete change prevented a recurrence?

rubric.hint: What did you learn?
rubric.follow_up: What is the biggest lesson you took from this?

hints: Interviewers look for ownership and learning, not perfection.

prompt: Tell me about a time you had to deliver under a tight deadline. How did you prioritize?

rubric.hint: What was the deadline and why was it tight?
rubric.follow_up: What made the deadline so tight?

rubric.hint: What did you choose not to do?
rubric.follow_up: What did you deliberately leave out, and how did you decide?

rubric.hint: Who did you keep informed?
rubric.follow_up: How did you set expectations with stakeholders?

rubric.hint: Did you make it? What happened next?
rubric.follow_up: What was the result, and was there any follow-up work?

hints: Prioritization and communication are the core signals.

prompt: Describe a time you helped a teammate grow or led an initiative without formal authority.

rubric.hint: What did you notice that needed doing?
rubric.follow_up: Why did you decide to take that on?

rubric.description: How you influenced or supported others
rubric.hint: How did you bring others along?
rubric.follow_up: How did you get buy-in without authority?

rubric.description: Impact on the person or team
rubric.hint: What changed because of it?
rubric.follow_up: How did you measure the impact?

hints: Focus on what you did and the measurable effect.

prompt: Walk me through the most technically interesting project on your resume: the problem, the architecture, your specific contribution, a key trade-off, and the result.

rubric.description: Explains the problem and why it mattered
rubric.hint: Start with who had the problem.
rubric.follow_up: Who was affected by the problem, and how did you know it mattered?

rubric.hint: Sketch the main components.
rubric.follow_up: How did data flow through the system?

rubric.hint: What did you do yourself?
rubric.follow_up: Which part did you personally design or build?

rubric.description: A real trade-off and alternatives considered
rubric.hint: What alternative did you reject?
rubric.follow_up: What alternative did you consider, and why did you reject it?

rubric.hint: What changed after it shipped?
rubric.follow_up: What measurable result did the project have?

hints: Be specific about your own role and one decision you made.

prompt: Tell me about the hardest bug you have debugged. How did you find the root cause?

rubric.hint: What did users or monitoring see?
rubric.follow_up: How did the bug show up, and how often?

rubric.hint: How did you narrow it down?
rubric.follow_up: How did you reproduce it, and how did you narrow down the cause?

rubric.hint: What was actually wrong?
rubric.follow_up: What exactly was the underlying cause?

rubric.hint: How did you prevent it recurring?
rubric.follow_up: What did you add so it could not happen again?

hints: Show a systematic process, not luck.
